path: Early October: Together holds second in polls; Eisenkot campaigns on integrity and security, gaining some centre-right voters, while Likud quietly welcomes the opposition split.
Mid October: Together frames the race as Bennett versus Netanyahu; swing voters start consolidating behind the list seen as most viable, which mostly favours Together over Yashar.
Oct 27 vote: Likud first, Together second with low twenties, Yashar around a dozen seats. No merger or late surge changes the order.
Early October: Together polls second behind Likud; Likud targets its right flank voters, Yashar courts the centre, but Together's machine and two leaders hold its base.
Mid October: Bennett-Lapid friction is contained; strategic voting tends to favour the largest opposition list rather than splitting it further; no polling collapse occurs.
Oct 27: Likud first, Together second, Yashar or the Arab joint list third. Together finishes second, not third.
After the first round Flávio consolidates the right and centrão, but governors give lukewarm endorsements; Lula leans on anti-Bolsonaro rejection and his Northeast base.
Debates and ads keep the race polarized; no major Lula health shock; polls show a close race with Lula slightly ahead.
Oct 25 runoff: result within a few points either way. A Flávio win by 8-12 points would need a large polling error and swing.
Netanyahu bloc polls around 50-54; the Jewish opposition 55-60; Arab lists near 10. Small lists like Smotrich's hover near the 3.25% threshold.
Campaign tightens; Haredi draft tensions persist; Arab turnout rises with the joint list, lowering both blocs' shares. No decisive security shock.
Oct 27: neither bloc reaches 61 unless a list falls below threshold and redistributes seats; most likely opposition near 57-59, right near 52.
Democrats pour money into Maine and Ohio; Iowa gets less. Collins runs on her independent brand, Husted on Trump support, Hinson on Iowa's red lean.
National environment favours Democrats moderately; Brown stays competitive, Platner leads Collins narrowly, Turek trails Hinson by mid-single digits.
Nov 3: Democrats likely win Maine, Ohio is close, Iowa stays Republican. Sweeping all three needs a wave.
Democrats defend three open seats in a midterm under a Republican president; Flanagan leads comfortably, Pappas edges Sununu, Michigan nominee tied or slightly ahead of Rogers.
Tariff and price discontent keep the environment Democratic-leaning; Rogers lacks Trump turnout; Sununu's brand keeps NH close.
Nov 3: Minnesota safe, NH and Michigan narrow Democratic wins most likely; a single upset in Michigan or NH is the main risk.
Remain campaign targets Calgary and Edmonton; separatists energize rural Alberta; Smith keeps leverage posture without campaigning for Leave.
Ottawa offers energy concessions; polls show Leave near 25-35%, giving Remain margins of roughly 30-50 points.
Oct 19 vote: Remain wins clearly, but Leave keeps a quarter to a third, so margin falls below 60 points.
Mid October: indirect US-Iran talks via Oman and Qatar continue; Trump wants lower gas prices but Iran avoids a formal deal that looks like surrender.
By Oct 23 only informal de-escalation and statements of progress; no qualifying joint acceptance announced. Senate races stay close with Republicans modestly favoured.
Nov 3: Republicans hold the Senate in most outcomes, losing Maine and perhaps one more but short of net four Democratic gains.
WTI elevated on Hormuz risk premium; Trump pushes SPR releases and OPEC+ output; partial shipping normalization trims prices.
Late October: oil hovers around the high seventies to mid eighties depending on Gulf news; no formal deal; Senate polls show Republicans modestly favoured.
Nov 2 close: roughly even odds oil is under $80; Republicans hold the Senate in about two-thirds of outcomes; both needed.
Indirect talks via Oman, Qatar and Pakistan continue; Trump hints a deal is close; Iran demands sanctions relief and rejects agreements under threat.
Informal de-escalation lets some shipping resume without a signed accord; Israel signals opposition; neither side declares acceptance of a formal agreement.
By Nov 2 no joint or matching acceptance announcements appear. A pre-election narrow shipping deal remains the main alternative path.
Oil stays elevated on Hormuz risk; Democrats push an expanded Senate map; high prices help Democrats while lower prices help the GOP, so legs conflict.
Late October: Democrats lead in Maine and North Carolina, competitive in Ohio, but need two more upsets; oil drifts near $80.
Nov 2-3: oil under $80 roughly even odds; Democratic Senate control about three in ten; joint outcome unlikely given negative correlation.
Oil eased from peaks but carries a Hormuz risk premium; Trump uses SPR and diplomacy to push prices down before the midterms.
No major new supply shock; WTI trades mostly below $85; Republicans keep a modest edge in Senate forecasting.
Nov 2: WTI likely under $85; Republicans hold the Senate in about two-thirds of outcomes; combined outcome slightly below even.
Trump seeks a pre-election Hormuz accord; Iran slow-walks formal agreement, preferring informal arrangements and sanctions relief first.
Talks produce statements of progress but no clear mutual acceptance; oil hovers around $80; Senate leans Republican.
By early November no qualifying deal; even with a deal, oil and Senate legs both needed. Triple outcome is unlikely.
Arab joint list campaigns on unity to lift turnout; polls show 10-14 seats, close to Yashar and Shas in the race for third and fourth.
Disqualification petitions fail in court; Arab turnout rises moderately; Yashar loses some voters to Together through strategic consolidation.
Oct 27: Likud and Together top two; joint list and Yashar compete for third. Joint list finishes fourth in a sizeable share of outcomes.
Mid October: indirect talks continue but Iran slow-walks; Trump presses for a quick shipping deal before the midterms.
Oct 23 passes without a formal joint acceptance announcement; only informal de-escalation steps reported.
The Hormuz leg fails in most worlds; even with a deal, oil under $80 and GOP Senate both required.
Democrats lead the generic ballot; mid-decade redistricting in Texas offsets partly by California's Prop 50 maps.
Election night Nov 3: Democrats gain seats in the East and Midwest; many close Western races remain uncounted for days.
AP calls control only once mathematically certain; with a large wave it could come by Nov 5-6, otherwise later as in 2022 and 2024.
Democrats expand targets, but Senate map offers few vulnerable Republican seats; House forecasts show gains in the twenties.
Late October environment stays Democratic-leaning but no historic collapse for Republicans; Osborn refuses to caucus with Democrats.
Nov 3: Democrats win the House with perhaps 225-240 seats and Senate near 49-51, well short of 250 and 54.
First election since Oct 7 and Iran wars; both camps mobilize; Haredi turnout high; Arab joint list pushes community turnout.
Campaign remains heated but voter rolls include many emigrants, depressing measured turnout; no election-day security disruption.
Oct 27: turnout rises to around 71-73%. Reaching 74% needs exceptional mobilization not seen since 1999.
Talarico raises record money against scandal-laden Paxton; Osborn runs a populist independent race; Marshall coasts in Kansas.
Late polls: Texas within a few points leaning Paxton, Nebraska Ricketts ahead mid-single digits, Kansas Marshall comfortably ahead.
Nov 3: all three must break against Republicans; Kansas almost certainly stays Republican, making the triple very unlikely.
Warsh prepares a scripted introductory statement; staff use a conventional opener, most likely 'good afternoon'.
Oct 28 press conference proceeds normally; Q&A covers inflation, rates, balance sheet; phrase could only appear incidentally.
Warsh says 'good afternoon' and 'thank you'; 'good day' is unlikely but possible as a sign-off or incidental phrase.
Brown leads in markets on his brand and a favourable environment; Husted relies on Ohio's red lean and Ramaswamy coattails.
Late October polls tighten in Ohio; a Husted-leading poll moves thin markets toward parity but Brown keeps a slight edge.
Before Nov 3 Husted may briefly overtake for a few hours; sustaining four consecutive hours above Brown is possible but less likely.
Talarico leads markets narrowly after record fundraising; GOP outside groups launch a big ad blitz for Paxton.
Polls show a near-tied race with Texas fundamentals reasserting; market odds converge toward parity.
In the final two weeks a Paxton-leading poll could flip the odds for four hours; flips in a thin, polarized market are plausible.
Hinson leads in markets on Iowa's red lean and funding; Turek campaigns on tariffs and farm pain.
Polls show Hinson ahead by mid-single digits; Democratic wave sentiment tightens but does not flip market odds.
Before Nov 3 a surprise Turek-lead poll could spike odds, but four consecutive hours ahead is unlikely.
Marshall comfortably ahead in Kansas; Hamilton underfunded with low name ID.
No shock poll or scandal; markets keep Marshall heavily favoured.
Window ends Oct 30 without Hamilton leading for four hours; only a manipulation spike could do it.
Ricketts self-funds heavily; Osborn raises well and courts crossover Republicans in an R+20 state.
Polls show Ricketts ahead by mid-to-high single digits; one tight poll lifts Osborn odds but not past Ricketts.
Before Nov 3 Osborn stays behind in markets; a four-hour lead needs an outlier poll and thin-market swing.
Marshall campaigns as incumbent; Hamilton targets Wichita suburbs with limited money.
Environment Democratic-leaning but Sedgwick's roughly 15-point Republican lean holds in federal races.
Nov 3: Marshall carries Sedgwick with a reduced margin; Democratic county win requires an unusual wave.
Oct 27 results: Likud largest; Together larger than Yashar; Netanyahu bloc short of 61 or near it.
Herzog consults parties; opposition recommendations largely go to Bennett as leader of the largest opposition list; Eisenkot backs Bennett for a senior role.
Herzog tasks Netanyahu or Bennett first; Eisenkot only if opposition unites behind him, which is unlikely.
Graham campaigns as Trump-endorsed incumbent; Democratic nominee underfunded; some MAGA discontent.
Greenville remains strongly Republican; any protest vote is small.
Nov 3: Graham carries Greenville County comfortably.
Acton condemns the ad and fundraises off it; Ramaswamy, combative, defends it publicly.
Media coverage continues; no clear polling backlash; Ohio GOP grumbles quietly. Ad rotation may end naturally, which does not count unless described as pulled.
By Oct 31 the ad is likely replaced in rotation without an announced withdrawal; explicit pull happens only if Acton's mother objects loudly.
Election night Nov 3: polls close in the East; safe-state results come quickly but don't settle control.
Key races in Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa, Texas, Alaska report later; several are close.
By 10:59 PM ET AP has not called Senate control; an early call needs a lopsided result unlikely this year.
